changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.sql: INSERT INTO EMAIL_CONTACT_ADDRESS (ID, CONTACT_ID, USER_ID, ADDRESS) SELECT ID, ID, USER_ID, PRIMARY_EMAIL FROM EMAIL_CONTACT WHERE PRIMARY_EMAIL IS NOT NULL

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment: A note is written in the platform's rich editor now, so what is stored is markup rather than bare text and the same paragraph costs several times the characters. Still bounded rather than a CLOB, for the reason the original column gives.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment: Changeset 1.0.0-34 seeded EMAIL_CONTACT_ADDRESS with explicit ids (each row taking its contact's), but SEQ_EMAIL_CONTACT_ADDRESS_ID was created at 1 and hands out ids one at a time. So on every vendor that draws ids from that sequence, the first addresses written after the upgrade are handed ids the seeded rows already hold, and the insert fails on the primary key — until the sequence has climbed past the largest seeded id, one failure at a time. It is not a slow burn either: the contact address repair runs at the first startup after the upgrade and writes through the same sequence. MySQL is left out on purpose: its auto-increment counter advances itself when a row arrives with an explicit id, which is why the bug is invisible on the vendor most deployments run.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
Drafts. A draft is a row of EMAIL_BOX like any other message, with FOLDER = 'DRAFTS' — not a table of its own. A conversation has to stay ONE query: the whole point of showing a draft is showing it at the bottom of the thread it belongs to, and a second table would mean every thread read became a join or a merge in Java, for the one row that matters most to the person reading.
Four columns is all the difference amounts to, and all four are null on every row that is not a draft.
DRAFT_LOCAL_ID is the handle the composer holds. It has to be OURS and it has to never change, because the only other candidate is the IMAP UID and that is not stable for a draft: IMAP cannot update a message, so saving a draft twice means appending a new message and deleting the old one, and the UID changes under the user mid-sentence. A UUID minted here survives that.
DRAFT_STATE is where the row stands against the server copy (see DraftState): it is what lets a save that changed nothing skip re-uploading the entire message, attachments included.
DRAFT_REVISION counts local edits. Autosaves are fired by a typing pause and travel over the network, so they can and do arrive out of order; the save path drops any that carries a revision the row has already passed. Without it a slow request carrying older text lands last and silently reverts the user's most recent sentence.
DRAFT_UPDATED_DATE is the local edit time, kept apart from RECEIVED_DATE on purpose even though the two are equal today. RECEIVED_DATE is what every ORDER BY in this schema sorts on, and once drafts join the sync it will hold the INTERNALDATE of the copy on the server; the moment the user last typed is a different fact and it is the one the reader should show.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment: Every draft read is "this user's draft with this local id" — the composer knows nothing else about the row. Not declared unique: uniqueness here would be enforced across a column that is null on every non-draft row, and vendors disagree about whether repeated nulls collide. The save path holds a per-draft lock instead, which is what actually serialises the writes.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
A draft that has not been uploaded has no IMAP UID, and MAIL_REMOTE_ID has been NOT NULL since 1.0.0-2. That was right for every row that had ever existed: each one mirrored a message on the server, and the UID was how it was addressed. A locally authored draft is the first row in this table that is not a copy of anything — it is written HERE and pushed up afterwards, so between the first keystroke and the first successful APPEND it has no UID to carry, which is the premise of the whole local-first design rather than an edge case. Slice 1 added the four draft columns and left this one alone, so the very first save of a new draft failed on the constraint.
A sentinel UID (0, -1) was considered and rejected. The code reasons in terms of "a UID means a copy exists on the server" — see EmailBoxService's serverDraftCopyUid, which is what the push, the discard and the send all ask before removing a copy — so a sentinel would have to be excluded again at every one of those questions, and at the sync's UID-keyed lookups (findByMailRemoteIdAndUserIdAndFolder, findCachedMailRemoteIds), where every unsent draft of a mailbox would collide on the one sentinel value. It would also not even be sufficient: detachDraftFromServerCopy writes MAIL_REMOTE_ID = NULL when the copy a row pointed at is gone from the server, so the column has to accept NULL regardless — the sentinel would only move the same failure later, into the sync, where it is far harder to see.
Dropping the constraint is additive and reversible: every existing row keeps its UID, and nothing that reads one starts having to handle a null it could not already get.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
Whether the cached body is HTML. The sync has always known — it reads the Content-Type of the part it takes the body from — and threw the answer away, so everything served from the cache claimed not to be HTML and the reader re-guessed it from the characters in the browser. It now travels with the row.
Deliberately nullable and deliberately without a default: null is the honest value for every row already cached, whose message was read before the column existed. Backfilling them with false would render every stored HTML mail as escaped source, and with true every plain-text mail would keep collapsing its line breaks — so the rows that were never asked stay unanswered, and the storage derives a value for those and only those. They age out of the cache on their own as the sync window moves.
Numbered 42 and not 39. This changeset was written against 38 while drafts was being written against the same 38, and drafts reached the databases first — 1.0.0-39 is already recorded there, with the drafts columns and the drafts checksum. Reusing the id would not have merged the two: Liquibase matches a changeset by id and author, finds it already ran, and either fails the checksum comparison or skips the changeset outright — leaving IS_HTML absent from a schema whose code reads it. The id moves; the column does not.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
The sequence EmailAttachmentEntity has been asking for since 1.0.0-5, and which was never created. Every other entity of this schema got one — 1.0.0-1 for the connector, 1.0.0-3 for the mail row, 1.0.0-16 for the contact, 1.0.0-33 for the contact address — and the attachment was simply missed.
It is not cosmetic on the vendors listed here. The entity declares @GeneratedValue(AUTO) against a named @SequenceGenerator, so on every dialect that HAS sequences Hibernate draws the id from SEQ_EMAIL_ATTACHMENT_ID, and the insert fails outright: "user lacks privilege or object not found". Which means that on PostgreSQL and Oracle, caching a message that carries an attachment cannot have been storing the attachment row at all.
MySQL is unaffected, and that is why this survived: it has no sequences, so Hibernate falls back to the table's own AUTO_INCREMENT and the ids come out fine. The same vendor asymmetry 1.0.0-38 documents for the contact-address sequence, from the other direction — it is the reason a defect in the id strategy is invisible on the vendor most deployments run.
Numbered 43 rather than 42: 42 is taken by the body-format branch, which is stacked on the same drafts work and not merged either. Two branches landing on one number is a reconciliation nobody should have to do twice.
Created starting at 1 rather than repaired past the existing rows, as 1.0.0-38 had to: no row can exist here on these vendors, precisely because the sequence never did. On a database where rows DO exist (one migrated from MySQL), the SequenceRepairChange of 1.0.0-38 is the tool, and it is deliberately not run here — it would be one more thing to get right for a case nobody has.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
Attachments on drafts, changesets 44 through 47. On the numbering, since it has already cost one reconciliation: the drafts work this is stacked on holds 39 to 41, the body-format branch — stacked on the same unmerged drafts work — holds 42, and 43 is the missing attachment sequence this branch's previous commit had to add before an attachment row could be written at all. So this group starts at 44. Anything landing after it starts at 48.
ATTACHMENT_REMOTE_ID is a MIME part path — "2" is the second part of the message this row belongs to — and it has been NOT NULL since 1.0.0-5 because every attachment that had ever existed here was a part OF a received message, and the path was how it was addressed.
A file the user attaches to a draft is the first one that is not. It is uploaded HERE, stored in the platform's file service, and only becomes a MIME part when the mail is finally sent — so between the paperclip and the Send button there is no part path to carry, which is the premise of the design rather than an edge case.
Exactly the reasoning 1.0.0-41 applied to MAIL_REMOTE_ID one changeset group earlier, for the same feature and the same reason: a locally authored row is not a copy of anything, so the columns that address the thing it copies are empty until it becomes one.
A sentinel path ("", "0") was considered and rejected on 1.0.0-41's grounds: the code asks "does this row name a part of a message" in several places, and a sentinel has to be excluded again at every one of them, while a null answers the question by being one.
Dropping the constraint is additive and reversible: every existing row keeps its path, and nothing that reads one starts having to handle a null it could not already get — the attachment lookups all match ON the path, so a null one is simply never returned by them.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
Where a draft's attachment actually lives. FILE_ID is the platform FileService id under the add-on's own namespace (EmailConnectorStorage NAME_SPACE), the same store contact photos and connector illustrations use — which is why nothing may ever sweep that namespace by "what the mail tables do not reference": it is shared, and the other two owners would lose their files.
The bytes are deliberately NOT a column. A BLOB here would put every attachment of every draft into the row a conversation read joins, and the thread query already fetches this table; the file service exists precisely so binary content is addressed by id and read on demand.
FILE_SIZE is denormalised from the file rather than joined for. The composer renders a size beside every chip and the send path caps a message's total, so it is read on every list and every send, and asking the file service per attachment for a number we already knew when we wrote it is a round trip per chip.
The index is on FILE_ID alone, and it is not there for the read path — nothing looks an attachment up by its file. It is for the sweep (a later slice), which has to answer "is this file still referenced by any row" for each marker it considers, and would otherwise scan the table once per marker.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
The orphan marker: a file that no row references any more, written down so that something can free it later.
It exists because of exactly how mail rows are deleted. EmailBoxDAO's deleteEmailsByIds is a bulk JPQL DELETE — no JPA cascade, no entity callbacks, no loaded instances — and the attachment rows go with it through the DATABASE-level ON DELETE CASCADE declared in 1.0.0-6. Nothing in Java ever observes that happening. So there is no lifecycle hook to hang "and free the file" on: it has to be explicit, and it has to read the file ids BEFORE the rows are gone, because afterwards nothing anywhere knows which files those were.
Two statements that cannot be one, therefore, and the order between them is the whole design. Recording first means a crash in between leaves a marker for a file that is still referenced — harmless, because the sweep verifies before it deletes. Deleting first would mean a crash leaves bytes in the file store that nothing names and nothing can ever find: a leak with no record of itself. A note nobody needed beats a file nobody can reach.
USER_ID is carried so the sweep can be scoped and its work attributed; it is deliberately not a foreign key, since the point of the row is to outlive everything it refers to.
FILE_ID is unique: recording the same file twice is a normal race (two cleanups over overlapping rows), and the second one should be a no-op rather than a second marker to process.
This changeset only creates the table, and this slice only WRITES to it. The sweep that reads it is a later slice; until then the markers accumulate, which is the point — they are the record that the work is outstanding.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment: The orphan marker's sequence, on the vendors that have sequences — created in the same breath as its table, which is the lesson 1.0.0-43 paid for.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
A written summary of one conversation, kept so it is produced once and read many times. Numbered 48 because 1.0.0-44's group announced that anything landing after it starts there, and this is the first thing that does.
It is a CACHE, not a record: every row here can be thrown away and rebuilt from the mail it describes. That is why there is no foreign key to EMAIL_BOX and no cascade -- a conversation's rows come and go as the sync window moves, and a summary written from the fuller conversation is still the better answer once the cache has trimmed its oldest messages.
Keyed by (USER_ID, THREAD_ID) rather than by THREAD_ID alone. A thread id is minted per mailbox out of the Message-IDs that mailbox holds, so two users on one mailing list legitimately produce the same id for what is, to each of them, their own copy of the conversation -- and a summary describes the copy it was written from. The uniqueness is an index rather than a compound primary key because every other table here is keyed by a generated id and the DAO layer expects one.
MESSAGE_COUNT and NEWEST_MESSAGE_KEY are the fingerprint of what was actually summarised, and they are the whole of the staleness rule: the read compares them against the conversation as it stands NOW, so nothing has to be scheduled and nothing has to be invalidated. NEWEST_MESSAGE_KEY is a folder and an IMAP UID ("INBOX:4217") rather than a date, because a date is not an identity -- two messages can share one, and a draft's changes on every keystroke.
SUMMARY is long text because it is prose about a whole conversation rather than a label. AGENT_NAME_ID records WHICH producer wrote it, so a deployment that changes producer can tell its old rows from its new ones instead of serving one voice as the other.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment: The summary's sequence, on the vendors that have sequences -- created in the same breath as its table, which is the lesson 1.0.0-43 paid for and 1.0.0-47 already had to repeat.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
EMAIL_ORPHAN_FILE's unique index, in its own changeset rather than beside the table in 1.0.0-46 -- and this separation is the whole point of the changeset, not tidiness.
modifySql is scoped to the CHANGESET, not to one change inside it. So the " ENGINE=INNODB CHARSET=... COLLATE ..." that 1.0.0-46 needs on its CREATE TABLE was also appended to the CREATE INDEX standing next to it, and MySQL rejects that clause on CREATE INDEX outright: error 1064, syntax error. Liquibase then stops on the failed changeset, the entityManagerFactory never builds, this add-on's Spring context never starts, and -- through the Kernel/Spring bridge -- the portal itself does not come up. One misplaced clause, the whole platform.
It was invisible everywhere except MySQL: modifySql carries dbms="mysql", so a developer on HSQLDB or PostgreSQL never generates the offending statement and sees the changeset apply perfectly. That is why this reached an acceptance server rather than a laptop, and why every index in this file from 1.0.0-19 onward already sits apart from any modifySql -- 1.0.0-33 keeps a table and its index together only because it appends nothing.
Guarded with a precondition because 1.0.0-46 can have got half way: MySQL commits DDL as it goes, so the CREATE TABLE stuck while the CREATE INDEX failed, and a failed changeset is never recorded. On such a database the table is already there and only this index is missing, which is exactly the state the MARK_RAN on 1.0.0-46 and the indexExists check here recover from -- no manual DROP, no data touched. On a database that ran the old 1.0.0-46 successfully (any non-MySQL one) the index exists already and this changeset marks itself ran.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
EMAIL_THREAD_AI_SUMMARY's unique index on (USER_ID, THREAD_ID), split out of 1.0.0-48 for the reason 1.0.0-50 sets out in full.
This one had not failed yet and would have: 1.0.0-46 halts the changelog before 1.0.0-48 is ever reached, so fixing only the first would have moved the same error one changeset along on the next restart. Both carried the same shape -- a createTable, a createIndex and a mysql modifySql in one changeset -- and they were the only two in this file that did.
The uniqueness is what makes a summary belong to one reader's copy of a conversation rather than to the thread id alone, so it is not optional: without the index two users on one mailing list would overwrite each other's summary.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
The registry of a user's own mail folders: the ones they made in their mailbox ("Factures", "Customers/Acme", a Gmail label), discovered by walking their IMAP folder list and mirrored here only once they have opted in.
Its ID is the whole point of the table. EMAIL_BOX.FOLDER stays the opaque VARCHAR(50) key it has always been and the third leg of (USER_ID, FOLDER, MAIL_REMOTE_ID); a custom folder's messages carry "CUSTOM:" plus this id. The remote name could not have been that key: it would not fit the column, a rename on the server would orphan every row, and a folder the user named "SENT" would collide with a constant. Nothing is added to EMAIL_BOX, no row of it is touched, and the existing (USER_ID, FOLDER, RECEIVED_DATE) index serves a CUSTOM key exactly as it serves ARCHIVE.
Three writers share a row, and the columns say which. DISPLAY_NAME, DELIMITER, MISSING and LAST_SEEN_DATE are discovery's. SYNC_ENABLED and ENABLED_DATE are the user's opt-in, from the settings screen. The five snapshot columns (UID_VALIDITY, UID_NEXT, MESSAGE_COUNT, HIGHEST_MODSEQ, WINDOW_SIZE) and LAST_SYNC_DATE are the sync job's: the folder's own change memory, kept here rather than in the JSON sync state so the least-recently-synced rotation and the skip-if-unchanged check read one row. The entity is DynamicUpdate for the same reason.
REMOTE_NAME is VARCHAR(500) rather than longer because it is half of a UNIQUE index beside a VARCHAR(250) USER_ID: on MySQL with utf8mb4 that pair is already 3000 of the 3072 bytes InnoDB allows a key, and an IMAP path of five hundred characters is not a folder anyone made by hand.
This table carries NO modifySql, unlike every table before it, and that is a decision and not an omission. Liquibase computes a changeset's checksum from its changes AND from its modifySql visitors, and a visitor is serialised through a filter that reads the checksum version off the CURRENT SCOPE, so the value depends on where it is computed: inside the update that executes the changeset it is one number, computed by anything that touched the parsed changelog earlier or elsewhere (a second Spring context on the same JVM) it is another, and the first computed value is the one a changeset remembers. That is how this very changeset, with a replace and an append on it, was recorded by one context and refused by the next in a single boot. Every earlier changeset that carries a modifySql has the same exposure; 1.0.0-5, -46 and -48 hide it behind validCheckSum ANY. So the MySQL table options and the collation this table needs live in 1.0.0-56, as literal SQL on a MySQL-only changeset, which is checksummed on its text and nothing else.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment: EMAIL_FOLDER's unique index on (USER_ID, REMOTE_NAME), apart from its table for the reason 1.0.0-50 sets out. The uniqueness is what makes a discovery walk an upsert: the same folder seen again finds its row, and the id the mirrored rows carry stays the same. Both columns ascending: this index serves equality lookups only, and the per-user listing it also prefixes is ordered in memory over a list bounded by the mailbox's folder count.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment: The registry's sequence, on the vendors that have sequences, created in the same breath as its table: the lesson 1.0.0-43 paid for, repeated by 1.0.0-47 and 1.0.0-49.

changeSet.author: email-connector
changeSet.comment:
What 1.0.0-53 would have said through a modifySql, said as SQL instead, for the reason 1.0.0-53's comment gives: literal SQL is checksummed on its text.
First the table options every table of this file gets on MySQL (InnoDB, utf8mb4, the accent-insensitive 0900 collation), applied after the fact. Then the one column that must NOT take that collation. REMOTE_NAME is an IMAP folder name, and an IMAP folder name is case-sensitive (RFC 3501 makes only INBOX an exception), as a Gmail label is: "Projets" and "projets" are two folders the unique index of 1.0.0-54 must keep apart. Under the accent- and case-insensitive collation the second would fail the index and, worse, the lookup by name would answer the FIRST folder's row, which the discovery walk would then keep renaming. utf8mb4_0900_bin rather than utf8mb4_bin because the older one is PAD SPACE (two names differing by a trailing space compare equal) while the 0900 family the table relies on is NO PAD; it needs MySQL 8.0.17.
Rolled back explicitly, because sql has no automatic rollback: the column goes back to the table's collation. The table options are not undone, they are what the server would have chosen anyway.
changeSet.sql: ALTER TABLE EMAIL_FOLDER ENGINE=INNODB, CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci
ALTER TABLE EMAIL_FOLDER MODIFY REMOTE_NAME VARCHAR(500) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_bin NOT NULL

rollback.sql: ALTER TABLE EMAIL_FOLDER MODIFY REMOTE_NAME VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL
